newsitem.title: USA: Conn official sees potential for pension bond sale.
newsitem.headline: Conn official sees potential for pension bond sale.

text.p: Connecticut's treasurer on Wednesday raised the possibility of the state selling pension obligation funds to pay for a switch to a less expensive form of retirement plan for state workers.
Christopher Burnham said: "Many people think I'm against pension obligation bonds. I'm, in fact, tolerant of pension obligation bonds used in the right situtation."
Burnham made the comments during an interview with Reuters Financial Television, parts of which will be shown on Thursday at 1515 EDT/1915GMT.

As examples of the types of plans he supported, Burnham cited Michigan's proposal to sell $3.6 billion of school pension bonds to pay for giving workers the option of switching to a defined contribution plan from a defined benefit plan. He also cited New Jersey's measure to capture a windfall from the state pension fund. "I only wish we in Connecticut had the guts to do what Michigan has done."

Connecticut has a clear economic motive for persuading its workers to bear more of the responsiblity of saving for their retirement. "We would save billions of dollars by going to a defined contribution plan," Burnham said.

He could not immediately estimate how big a pension bond sale would be needed to change retirement plans, and noted that the proposal would face an uphill battle. "I think we have to take a very long-term view on this because we'll continue to see union opposition to making their members millionaires," Burnham said, when asked if such a measure would be submitted next year.

The treasurer said state employees also stood to gain by moving to a defined contribution plan, as individuals who start saving while still in their 20s could expect to retire with large sums of money. He added workers could do a better job managing their investments than elected state officials. However, he predicted union leaders would resist the move.

The state's unfunded pension liability totals about $5.5 billion, and Gov John Rowland and the legislature agreed a 35-year amortization schedule to close the gap. The pension fund has performed strongly under Burnham's leadership, growing to $16 billion from $10.5 billion in his two-and-a-half years in office. "I expect to end the fiscal year on June 30 with a very strong showing," he added, noting 78 percent of the fund is invested in stock indexes, and the market has risen 20 percent in the last three months.

Burnham said he also could support having Connecticut sell pension obligation bonds for a handful of municipalities that face sizable unfunded pension liabilities, provided that the state kept strict control of the funds raised and handled the investments. "There may also be a time when we will have to issue these bonds for municipalities that have excessive unfunded liablities because they so screwed up their budgets or pension fund management, or both, in the past."
